Resonance of Silence

About This Experience

A mobile audio-description experience for blind and deaf viewers: Resonance of Silence

Audio description for everyone — a dialogue between two statues, the Pensive Bodhisattva and The Thinker, to be enjoyed like watching a film.

Why This Experience Is Different

Most art appreciation is built on the premise of "seeing." This experience begins from the opposite premise — it is designed around spoken audio description, captions, and a touch-based AI chatbot, so that blind viewers can enjoy it from start to finish on their own, without a screen reader and without a companion.

Placing the Eastern Pensive Bodhisattva and the Western Thinker side by side, the experience is organized into two parts comparing two attitudes: a "difficult mind" and a "warm mind."

Part 1 · Encounter

With the images of Rodin's The Thinker and the Pensive Bodhisattva side by side on screen, you follow the audio description as if watching a film, grasping first the form and posture of the two statues, then their meaning. The narration uses a pyramid structure, giving the whole picture first, then detailed explanations of each part.

Part 2 · Contemplation and Embodiment

Tapping a part of either statue image on screen — forehead, hand, foot, and so on — plays an audio description of that spot's meaning, and any further questions can be asked freely to an AI chatbot. You can also mirror the statues' poses, experiencing the work with your whole body.

Between the Two Statues — At the Edge of Color

"Looking at the two statues side by side on one screen, a tremor arises at the boundary, as in a work by Mark Rothko." The Pensive Bodhisattva's warm gilt-bronze glow and the deep brown of Rodin's bronze The Thinker. Facing that gap of contrasting color and space, viewers face a shiver much like standing before one of Rothko's vast color-field abstractions.

The Ambiguity of the Boundary, and Its Resonance

Just as Rothko's canvases blur their edges and draw the viewer into a depth of color, the point where the Bodhisattva's radiant gold and the Rodin bronze's heavy darkness cross generates a subtle wave that reaches beyond mere physical distance. The spatial tension and emotional stir felt while gazing at the space between the two statues is the vibration of a boundary where Eastern and Western thought meet.

Where Materiality Meets Color Field

The rough texture of time-worn brown bronze, and the softly glowing surface of gilt-bronze that has carried its shine across a thousand years. The quiet yet overwhelming energy of these two materials meets the boundlessness of color without edges, drawing viewers into deep emotional immersion. This resonance, rising out of silence, becomes a sensory experience absorbed by the whole body — beyond what the eyes alone can take in.

Planning/Production

Overall direction and digital interaction — Jun-Dong Cho (Professor Emeritus, Sungkyunkwan University)
Disability accessibility — Geun-Hae Yuk (Director, Institute for Accessibility Research for the Disabled)

Accessibility Features

WCAG 2.1 AA compliant — designed to meet international web accessibility standards.
Screen-reader support — supports TalkBack and VoiceOver, narrating all on-screen information aloud.
Audio description — tap a statue image on screen to hear that scene and its meaning in spoken narration and captions.
AI voice conversation — an AI chatbot lets viewers freely ask and hear answers to their questions.

Philosophy (Humartology)

Grounded in the Humartology philosophy — the fusion of Human, Art, and Technology — this experience dissolves the boundary between disabled and non-disabled viewers, realizing an aesthetics of accessibility where everyone can equally access a thousand years of contemplation.

Part 2 Artwork Introduction — Meaning and Contemplation, Part by Part

Title — Resonance of Silence: Contemplation and Embodiment

This experience extends Donald Norman's three levels of emotional design (visceral, behavioral, and reflective) into three aesthetic stages through which the viewer comes to feel a connection with the artwork: Encounter, Embodiment, and Yeoil (Oneness). Encounter (an emotional approach) uses a multisensory interface combining sight, hearing, and on-screen touch to convey the intense sensory impact of the viewer's first meeting with the artwork. Embodiment (a behavioral approach) lets the meaning of the artwork naturally soak into the viewer's own body and actions, through physical interaction — tapping parts of the statue images to hear about them, and imitating their poses with one's own body. Yeoil (a reflective approach) brings past and present ways of thinking together as one (如一), completing a time of reflection filled with deep inner calm and inspiration.

Part 2 is not about the overall form, but about tapping, part by part, into the meaning and contemplation held in each spot. Exploring the same kind of place — brow, hand, posture, foot — on the Gilt-Bronze Pensive Bodhisattva (Maitreya) and on Rodin's The Thinker, you discover how differently each statue has written its mind into that one spot.

In The Thinker, an unreleased weight is condensed into the brow, the clenched fist, the elbow, the tensed muscles of the back — moments of what Spinoza called conatus, the basic effort of a being to persist in its own existence, still colliding forcefully with the outside world. In the Pensive Bodhisattva, that same weight has been set down at the ear, the smile, the fingers, the folds of drapery, the seated pose, the toes — moments that have slipped free of affliction and touched an unconditioned "joy of cessation." Like the two halves of the old saying "do all you can, then leave the rest to heaven": Rodin's toes, still gripping the ground, are the "doing all you can" that hasn't yet let go; the Bodhisattva's toes, fully at ease, are the "leaving it to heaven" that already has.

Each time you tap a single part in Part 2, this difference between the two minds will reach you through the audio description.

Gilt-Bronze Pensive Bodhisattva (Maitreya)

A Buddhist sculpture estimated to have been made during the Three Kingdoms period (6th-7th century), depicting Maitreya, the bodhisattva who will save all beings in the future, absorbed in deep contemplation. It is notable for the half-lotus posture, right foot resting on the left knee, and fingers lightly touching the cheek. The two most representative examples, held by the National Museum of Korea, were once designated National Treasure No. 78 and No. 83, respectively; today they are labeled simply as National Treasures, without numbers.

The Pensive Bodhisattva — the summit of Korea’s bronze-casting tradition

If Rodin was compared to Michelangelo for pushing past the conventions of modern sculpture, the Gilt-Bronze Pensive Bodhisattva is counted among the greatest masterpieces of East Asian Buddhist sculpture of the sixth and seventh centuries. The pensive form began in India and passed through China, where such figures usually served as attendants beside a main image; Three Kingdoms artisans instead raised the pose into an independent gilt-bronze icon nearly a meter tall. In the painter Sam Gilliam’s words, “It’s not about making something new, it’s about making something your own” — and the Pensive Bodhisattva is the clearest case of a borrowed form made fully Korea’s own.

That delicacy did not appear from nowhere. In the Bronze Age, the finely lined bronze mirror (Danyu Semungyeong) carried more than 13,000 lines spaced about 0.3 millimeters apart on a disc just over 21 centimeters wide — precision hard to reproduce even today. On that tradition, this 93.5-centimeter figure was cast around a single iron core running from head to feet, with walls averaging about one centimeter, and so finely that it shows almost no repairs. Where Chinese pensive figures render the drapery over the seat in a stiff, formulaic way, the folds here are praised for flowing like real cloth. The fingers hovering just short of the cheek are the lightest moment hard metal can hold.

The wooden Pensive Bodhisattva of Kōryū-ji in Kyoto resembles this figure down to the crown and the modeling of chest and waist, and is treated as a leading example of how sculpture from the Korean peninsula carried across the sea to Japan. Japan carved the pose in wood; this figure was poured in metal. And while Rodin’s Thinker was cast many times from plaster models and spread around the world, the Pensive Bodhisattva is one of a kind.

Mark Rothko believed art could reach “the heights of exaltation as well as the depths of despair.” If The Thinker bears those depths with his muscles, the Pensive Bodhisattva crosses the same thought in the stillness of a faint smile. Rashid Johnson has said that “consciousness can be a medium.” Here the gilt bronze is only the material; the true medium is contemplation itself. As Spencer Finch puts it, rather than revealing truths, this smile creates a situation that reveals the world “in a subtle and complex way.”

Robert Irwin wrote that “seeing is forgetting the name of the thing one sees.” Set aside the names — National Treasure, gilt bronze, Three Kingdoms — and simply listen. In Lygia Pape’s words, an artwork exists “not as a finished and resolved object, but as something that is always present, permanent within people.” This smile has lasted fourteen hundred years not in the metal, but within people.

Sources · National Museum of Korea [15] · Kyunghyang Shinmun [16][17] · Wikipedia [18] · Quotations: Mark Rothko [19]; Sam Gilliam, Rashid Johnson, Spencer Finch, Robert Irwin, Lygia Pape [20] (see References)

Gilt-Bronze Pensive Bodhisattva (Maitreya) — Artist Unknown

Believed to have been made by the hand of a Three Kingdoms-period artisan, but the artist's name has not been passed down.

The Thinker (Le Penseur)

First created around 1880 by the French sculptor Auguste Rodin as a figure atop The Gates of Hell, then recast in 1904 as an independent, large-scale bronze. A masterpiece of modern sculpture expressing, through tensed muscle and a hunched posture, the difficult mind a person carries through life.

According to the National Gallery of Art, Rodin pushed sculpture beyond previously accepted rules of finish and anatomical correctness; his fiercely expressive treatment of the figure led to comparisons with Michelangelo, and his broken, roughly finished surfaces were compared to the innovations of the impressionists. He modeled his ideas in clay or wax with his own hands, had plaster casts made, and employed specialists to enlarge, reduce, and cast them in bronze. The Thinker thus became a veritable best-seller in his lifetime and is now spread across collections around the world. [14]

Auguste Rodin (1840-1917)

French sculptor. Left behind works such as The Burghers of Calais and The Gates of Hell, and is credited with opening a new chapter in modern sculpture through the realistic rendering of the human body and rough surface texture.

How to Use

① Getting started — Tap the first screen once to hear the introduction, and once more to begin (it also starts automatically after one minute if you don't tap). Use the Music button on this screen to turn background music on or off before starting.

② Viewing — Tap (click/touch) any part you're curious about on the statue images on screen, and a short audio description of that part plays immediately in voice and captions — tapping a part is the one exception that responds on a single tap. When using a phone camera to recognize your hand, the vibration rhythm the moment your fingertip reaches a part on screen tells you its rough shape — short and dense means a rounded, clustered part (like a fist), a long continuous buzz means an elongated part (arm, ear, robe fold), two very short pulses means a narrow, pointed part (finger, toe), and a slow, gentle wave means a broad, flat part (forehead, face). Press the 💬 button on the right-center of the screen to open the "Contemplation Counsel" chatbot (you can also press and drag this button to move it wherever you like). Tap a ready-made suggested question to ask without typing, or type or use the microphone button to ask freely about the part you just tapped or either statue. The first time you use the microphone, your phone asks for permission; choose “Allow while visiting the site” and it won’t ask again. Personal questions like worry or life are answered side by side, in each statue's own voice — if you're currently exploring a part, the answer draws on that part's story, and this is not historical fact but a creative interpretation voiced by the two statues. Asking "summarize what I've explored so far" gives you your record so far, plus how many parts you still haven't explored. When you touch a part of one statue, that statue grows larger around your fingertip, so the part stays under your finger and nearby parts are easier to find. Touch the empty space in the middle, a blank area, or the Show both sculptures button to return to the full view.

③ Playback controls — If you missed an explanation while following the image, you can always hear it again by tapping the same part again or pressing the Replay button at the bottom of the screen. Most other buttons (Certificate, Serenity, Part 1, 💬, etc.) speak their name and glow gold on the first press; pressing the same button again within a few seconds actually activates it. The ⓘ info button, the Speed and Easy sentences buttons, and the background music volume slider respond immediately on press or movement, with no second press needed.

⑤ Fingertip explore — Press the Fingertip button at the bottom to open a large photo of one statue. Slowly slide your fingertip over it: inside the statue you hear a tone that rises as you go up, and where the form juts forward, sound and vibration grow stronger. Reaching a part speaks its name and vibrates as many times as its number. Switch between the Pensive Bodhisattva and The Thinker at the top, or move through the parts list below.

④ Moving elsewhere — Press the Certificate button (twice) any time to see your record of what you've encountered so far. Pressing the Print button on the certificate screen twice saves it as a PDF file. Pressing the Serenity button (twice) moves you to a mind-clearing screen — after listening to the guidance through to the end, you must press either the Part 1 or Part 2 button shown on that screen yourself to actually move. Pressing the Part 1 button at the bottom (twice) skips this and goes straight to Part 1 any time. The chat panel closes when you press the ✕ button at its top, or by swiping from left to right. This info panel returns one step at a time — from a detail screen back to the menu, or from the menu back to the viewing screen — when you press the Return button at the bottom, or swipe from left to right. If you're using a keyboard, Esc also closes either the info panel or the chat panel right away.

If you use a screen reader, the artwork narration is read by the built-in voice, and buttons and short notices by your screen reader. Please lift your finger from the screen while the narration plays.
